7. Strike-free periods

The sector rules set periods, around the busiest travel dates, when transport strikes are not allowed. The first and last day of each period are included.

PeriodTrainsFlightsLocal transport
Christmas and New Year18 Dec – 7 Jan18 Dec – 7 Jan17 Dec – 7 Jan
EasterThursday before to Thursday afterThursday before to Thursday after5 days before and after
Late April holidays24 Apr – 2 May24 Apr – 2 Maynone
Early summer27 Jun – 4 Jul27 Jun – 4 Jul27 Jun – 4 Jul
Summer27 Jul – 3 Sep27 Jul – 5 Sep28 Jul – 3 Sep
All Saints30 Oct – 5 Nov30 Oct – 5 Nov30 Oct – 5 Nov

There are also periods around national and European elections and referendums (from three days before to three days after the vote), with shorter periods for local elections in the areas that vote.

Lower risk, not zero risk

These are the rules; the register shows what has actually been announced. In October 2026, for example, the register listed a national general strike, including trains, on 30 October, the first day of the All Saints period. So treat these periods as quieter, not as a guarantee, and check the register as usual.

Sources: rail, national agreement of 23 November 1999 (consolidated text), point 3.5.1; air, provisional rules of the Commissione di garanzia, resolution 14/387 of 13 October 2014, article 8, published by ENAC; local transport, national agreement of 28 February 2018 assessed by the Commissione di garanzia (resolution 18/138), article 4. Texts read on 10 October 2026.

8. Why rail strikes start at 21:00

The rail rules say that a strike may last at most 24 hours, and that 24-hour strikes must start at 21:00. The first strike in a dispute may last at most eight hours, either from 09:01 to 17:59 or from 21:01 to 05:59. That is why you so often see "dalle 21.00" in the register, and why a strike "on Friday" usually begins on Thursday evening.

Other sectors have similar limits. In local transport, the first strike in a dispute may not exceed four hours, and two strikes affecting the same area must be at least 20 days apart. In air transport, the first strike may last at most four hours, the minimum notice is twelve days, and strikes affecting the same service and area must be at least fifteen clear days apart (thirty for air traffic control).

Sources: rail agreement of 1999, points 3.3.1 and 3.3.2; local transport rules of 2018, articles 11 and 12; air transport rules 14/387, articles 4, 7, 16 and 17. Read on 10 October 2026.
faq_franchigie: Not exactly, but there are strike-free periods around Christmas, Easter, late April, the summer holidays and All Saints, set by the rules of each sector. They lower the risk without removing it (chapter 2).
rimborsi_operatori:
What Trenitalia and Italo pay for delays

The companies' own conditions follow the EU levels and, in some cases, add to them:

Delay at arrivalTrenitaliaItalo
30 to 59 minutesFrecce: a bonus of 25% of the ticket price, to use within 12 monthsnone
60 to 119 minutes25% of the ticket price25% of the ticket price
120 minutes or more50% of the ticket price50% of the ticket price
  • Trenitalia: claim within one year of the delay. On regional trains the 25% applies to tickets of at least €16 and the 50% to tickets of at least €8. Trenitalia does not pay amounts under €4 per passenger (Italian page).
  • Italo: paid as a voucher or to the Italo wallet within 30 days of the request.

Italo on strike days: read this

Italo's conditions (article 16.1) say that during a strike, a train Italo has marked "not guaranteed" does not count as "cancelled", so the remedies Italo provides for cancelled trains do not apply to it. If your Italo train is marked "not guaranteed", do not wait: check Italo's strike notice and change or cancel your booking early, under the options it offers.

Sources: Trenitalia, "Compensation for delays and refund" (English) and "Indennità per ritardo" (Italian); Italo, general conditions of carriage valid from 1 October 2026, articles 16.1 and 16.3. Checked 10 October 2026.
